title: The Stone Face
description: Smith's fourth and last novel, published by Farrar, Straus on 7 November 1963 and described by its publisher in 2021 as a roman a clef: an African American journalist who has fled racist violence in Philadelphia finds freedom in Paris, then recognises in the treatment of Algerians the racism he escaped. It is one of the earliest published accounts of the Paris massacre of 17 October 1961 (Kirkus; New York Review Books; Wikipedia).
plot_or_argument: As a teenager in Philadelphia Simeon Brown lost an eye in a racist attack, and the young journalist has lived ever since in a state of agonising tension; after a violent encounter with white sailors he moves to Paris, known as a haven for Black artists and intellectuals, where he can go where he pleases without fear (New York Review Books). Through Babe, another Black American emigre, he makes friends among the interracial expatriates and falls in love with a Polish actress, who proves to be Jewish and to have spent her childhood in concentration camps (NYRB; Kirkus). Through chance-met Algerians, treated more brutally in Paris than Black people in America, he slowly comes to see race hatred, the 'stone face' of the title, as universal and irrational rather than personal, its victims changing from country to country, and his expatriate friends begin to pall. Simeon joins the Algerians in a riot; finally, 'no longer an escapist nor a member of a separate race', he leaves to become a teacher (Kirkus). Wikipedia, citing Kristin Ross, calls the novel's account of the Paris massacre of 17 October 1961 one of the earliest eyewitness representations of it, though fictionalised.
narrative_structure: Follows Simeon from the violence that drives him out of Philadelphia, through his life among expatriates and Algerians in Paris, to his decision to leave (Kirkus; NYRB).
principal_characters: Simeon Brown; Babe; the Polish actress; Simeon's Algerian friends
meter_and_prosody: Kirkus called it 'somewhat didactic, naive, but basically quite interesting', its 'rather flat prose' redeemed by 'some fine oblique scenes and a few shocking comparisons between various ghettos, concentration camps, riots and tortures'.
historical_context: Smith began the novel in 1961, when the Algerian War had inflamed passions in France, and drew on the anti-Arab racism he witnessed as a journalist and in the streets of Paris; Kristin Ross writes that it was published in the United States because it could not be published in France (Wikipedia).
literary_significance: Ross notes that it remained one of the few representations of 17 October 1961 available until the early 1990s, when the children of North African immigrants began to demand information about the event. Kirkus called it 'a thought-provoking and an oddly humanizing and liberating book', and New York Review Books reissued it in 2021 with an introduction by Adam Shatz (Wikipedia; Kirkus).
bibliographical_notes: New York: Farrar, Straus, 7 November 1963 (Kirkus; Wikipedia); New York Review Books Classics, 2021, introduction by Adam Shatz (ISBN 978-1-68137-516-8).
thematic_analysis: The universality of race hatred, seen by a Black American who finds that in France he is simply an American while the Algerians bear the racism he fled; bystander guilt and solidarity, the subject of Alexa Weik von Mossner's chapter on Smith; the memory of the Holocaust carried by his lover; and the choice between personal freedom and political engagement.
summary: Simeon Brown, a Black American journalist who lost an eye in a racist attack as a teenager, settles in Paris, falls in love with a Polish actress who survived the concentration camps, befriends Algerians, joins them in a riot, and finally leaves to become a teacher.
